sections.h2: How does probate work in Kansas?
sections.html:
Probate in Kansas is a court process run through the district court, and its job is to prove a will, name someone to manage the estate, pay valid debts and pass the rest to the people entitled to it. Kansas Legal Services notes that all probate proceedings are subject to the authority of the district court, and that juries are not used in these matters.

If the person left a will, it names an executor. If there is no will, the court appoints an administrator. Either one is personally responsible for handling the estate properly, which includes notifying heirs and creditors, inventorying and protecting the assets, paying taxes and valid claims, and distributing what is left. The same Kansas Legal Services guide says appointing an executor usually takes four to five weeks from the day the petition is filed, though no two estates run on the same schedule.

For anyone who inherited a house, the practical point is simple: until a personal representative has been appointed, nobody has clear authority to sign a sale contract for the estate. Kansas Legal Services also warns that a person who deals with the dead owner's property without a formal court appointment can be held personally responsible for what they do.

sections.h2: What deadlines apply to a Kansas probate?
sections.html:
Four dates matter most to a family that is thinking about selling an inherited house: the six-month window to file a will, the 30-day publication step, the four-month creditor period and the small estate ceiling of $75,000. The table below lists each one with the rule behind it.

ItemWhat the rule saysSource
Filing a will for probateA will does not pass property unless a petition is filed within six months of the deathK.S.A. 59-617
Publishing notice to creditorsPetitioner must give notice within 30 days after filing, once a week for three consecutive weeks, in a county newspaperK.S.A. 59-709, as amended in 2024
Creditor claim windowFour months from first publication, or 30 days after actual notice to a known creditor if that is laterK.S.A. 59-2239
Small estate affidavitPersonal property can move without letters when probate assets are $75,000 or lessK.S.A. 59-1507b
Earliest closingAn estate with assets beyond allowances and debts cannot close before six months after deathKansas Legal Services

The 30-day figure is a recent change. A 2024 law (Senate Bill 379) lengthened the publication deadline from 10 days to 30 days after the petition is filed. Older articles and forms may still show the shorter number.

sections.h2: What property goes through probate, and what skips it?
sections.html:
Only property titled in the dead person's name alone, with no beneficiary or survivor rights attached, normally goes through probate. Kansas Legal Services lists several kinds of property that bypass it:

  • Property held in joint tenancy with right of survivorship
  • Life insurance paid to a named beneficiary other than the estate
  • Bank accounts with a pay on death designation
  • Assets with transfer on death provisions, including securities, titled vehicles and real estate

That last item matters for houses. If the owner recorded a transfer on death deed before dying, the house passes to the named beneficiary outside the estate. Our guide to the Kansas transfer on death deed covers how those deeds work. If no such deed or survivorship title exists, the house is a probate asset.

sections.h2: Can an executor sell the house during probate?
sections.html:
Yes, and the route depends on what the will says. Under K.S.A. 59-1413, if a will authorizes the executor to sell property, the executor may use that power without an order of the district court, unless the will provides otherwise. The power cannot be used while a proceeding to contest the will or to probate a later will is pending.

A buyer in good faith who takes title under that power gets the real estate free of the creditors' liens and claims against the estate and the heirs. Those claims move to the sale proceeds. Tax liens are the exception, and the statute says the transfer does not affect them.

When the will gives no power of sale, or there is no will, the administrator petitions the court instead. K.S.A. 59-2303 lets the petition name a prospective purchaser and the proposed terms, ask the court to approve appraisers and ask it to confirm the deal. If the buyer is related to the fiduciary by blood or finances, the petition has to say so. If there is no relationship, the petition says that instead.

The court path also has a public auction option. Notice of an auction of real estate must run once a week for three consecutive weeks in a county newspaper, and the sale date falls no sooner than 10 days and no later than 30 days after the last publication (K.S.A. 59-2308). Many families prefer a negotiated private sale for that reason.

sections.h2: What does a small estate affidavit cover, and what does it leave out?
sections.html:
The small estate affidavit in K.S.A. 59-1507b covers personal property only, so it does not move title to a house. When a Kansas resident dies with probate assets of $75,000 or less, a successor can give a bank or other holder an affidavit and collect personal property without letters of administration. The 2024 amendment also lets the property go to a person claiming to be a successor, or as that successor directs.

Real estate needs a different step. Kansas Legal Services explains that when someone dies without a will and leaves only real estate, a determination of descent proceeding can be started any time six months after death, and it typically takes about 30 days. That proceeding is how heirs obtain a court record of who owns the house before they sell.

The Kansas courts' self-help probate page links the Judicial Council forms, including the small estates affidavit, and points readers to their local district court for questions.

sections.h2: What costs and taxes come with a Kansas estate?
sections.html:
Fees for the executor and the lawyer are not fixed by law. Kansas Legal Services says they must reflect the fair value of the work compared with the size of the estate, and the probate court approves them. Court fees are set by law, and publication charges and a bond premium may be added.

Property tax keeps running while the estate is open. Kansas real estate tax is due in full by December 20, or in two halves, with the second half due May 10 of the next year (K.S.A. 79-2004). Unpaid amounts draw interest at the statutory rate plus five percentage points. A house that sits through a long probate can pick up a tax bill and interest before anyone sells it. Our Kansas property tax guide walks through the calendar.

Kansas Legal Services adds that a transfer on death deed does not avoid creditors, and it recommends that an executor not prepare the estate's tax returns without a lawyer's help.

sections.h2: What should heirs do first when a house is part of the estate?
sections.html:
Protect the house, call a probate lawyer and gather the paperwork, in that order. Kansas Legal Services advises that nothing should be done to disturb the dead person's property unless it is needed to keep it from being lost or destroyed, and that a lawyer should be contacted soon after the death, with the will in hand at the first meeting.

  • Locate the original will and note the date of death, since the six-month filing window starts there.
  • Find the recorded deed. Check whether it shows joint tenants or a transfer on death beneficiary.
  • List the mortgage, tax and utility accounts, and note the next property tax due date.
  • Ask the lawyer whether the will gives the executor a power of sale, since that changes whether a court order is needed.
  • Decide among the heirs who will sign, because every owner or the court-appointed representative must agree to a sale.

sections.h2: How does a cash sale fit into a Kansas probate?
sections.html:
A cash purchase fits at the point where the personal representative has authority, and the sale proceeds then pass through the estate account to creditors and heirs. A cash buyer can close without waiting on a bank's loan approval, which removes one source of delay in an estate that already has court steps to finish.

We buy houses as-is, so an inherited property that needs repairs, has personal belongings left in it or sits vacant can still be considered. The title company handling the closing will want to see the court's appointment of the executor or administrator and, where the will does not grant a power of sale, the court's order. Ask the estate's lawyer to confirm which documents apply to your file before you sign anything.

faqs.q: How long does probate take in Kansas?
faqs.a: There is no fixed length. Kansas Legal Services says appointing an executor usually takes four to five weeks after filing, creditors have four months, and an estate with assets beyond allowances and debts cannot close before six months after the date of death. Many estates run longer.

faqs.q: Can I sell an inherited house in Kansas before probate is finished?
faqs.a: Sometimes. If the will gives the executor a power of sale, no court order is needed under K.S.A. 59-1413. Without that power, the administrator asks the district court for approval under K.S.A. 59-2303. Either way a court-appointed representative must exist first.

faqs.q: Does a small estate affidavit transfer a house in Kansas?
faqs.a: No. K.S.A. 59-1507b covers personal property when probate assets are $75,000 or less. Real estate needs probate or a determination of descent, unless a transfer on death deed or survivorship title already controls it.

faqs.q: How many days does a creditor have to file a claim?
faqs.a: Four months from the first publication of notice, or 30 days after actual notice to a known or reasonably ascertainable creditor if that is later (K.S.A. 59-2239). Claims presented after that are barred.

faqs.q: Do I need a lawyer for a Kansas probate?
faqs.a: The law does not say every estate needs one, but Kansas Legal Services recommends contacting a lawyer soon after a death and says an executor should not prepare tax returns without a lawyer's guidance. This page is general information and not legal advice.
